Zygomatic trauma

One controlled study reports sensory improvement after delayed treatment, and one randomized trial reports less postoperative swelling. These are distinct outcomes and do not establish a consistent recovery benefit.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One controlled study reports sensory improvement after delayed treatment, and one randomized trial reports less postoperative swelling. These are distinct outcomes and do not establish a consistent recovery benefit.

Summary of the Evidence

Two human reports directly address zygomatic trauma: one exact-category controlled clinical report (71 participants; the database labels it single-arm with case/control subgroups) and one randomized zygomaticomaxillary-complex fracture trial (46 participants) indexed under oral trauma/fractures. No animal or in-vitro study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Bashiri et al. reported sensory improvement after delayed PBM, but a database comment notes similar changes in the case and control groups, limiting confidence. Jain et al. reported less postoperative swelling after LLLT. The studies assess different outcomes and do not establish a reproducible benefit (Bashiri et al. 2021; Jain et al. 2026). In the 71-participant controlled report, the database classifies the design as a single-arm study with case/control subgroups; these groups should not be treated as randomized. The separate 46-participant randomized trial evaluates postoperative swelling, not sensory nerve recovery, so it adds trauma context without replicating the same endpoint. The two reports do not provide a common estimate for zygomatic-fracture recovery.

Primary original studies: Bashiri et al. 2021 Jain et al. 2026

Animal evidence

none identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Bashiri et al. report an 810 nm diode protocol at 27 J/cm², 200 mW, and 12 points over 12 sessions in 6 weeks. Jain et al. report 810 nm treatment at 500 mW twice daily for 4 days. These are near-infrared wavelengths, outside visible light. The different outcomes and schedules should not be combined into one regimen.

Interpretation

The sensory study used controlled groups but was not reported as randomized, and the fracture trial measured swelling rather than nerve recovery. Small samples, different endpoints, and different schedules make the signals preliminary. Neither study establishes improved long-term function, fracture union, or superiority to usual postoperative care.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. Two controlled studies report possible sensory or swelling benefits on different outcomes.
Publications and records2 unique titles.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small clinical studies examine different outcomes after zygomatic trauma. A parallel controlled study reports sensory changes after delayed treatment, while a separate randomized fracture trial assesses postoperative swelling. The designs and endpoints do not replicate one another, and the available reports do not establish a reproducible effect on overall fracture recovery.
